plancks-law-for-spectral-energy-density-.title: Planck's Law for Spectral Energy Density of Black-Body Radiation
plancks-law-for-spectral-energy-density-.conceptual_definition: This formula describes the spectral energy density $u_$ u($T$)$ of electromagnetic radiation inside a black-body cavity in thermal equilibrium at a given absolute temperature $T$, as a function of frequency $u.
plancks-law-for-spectral-energy-density-.intuitive_summary: It quantifies how much energy is contained in electromagnetic waves of a specific frequency (color) within a hot, enclosed space, explaining the distribution of light emitted by hot objects.
plancks-law-for-spectral-energy-density-.interpretation: This law was a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, introduced by Max Planck in 1900 to resolve the 'ultraviolet catastrophe' predicted by classical physics. It postulates that electromagnetic energy is not emitted or absorbed continuously but in discrete packets (quanta) of energy $E = h u$. The formula is derived by considering the electromagnetic modes within a cavity and applying Bose-Einstein statistics to the photons, which are indistinguishable bosons with zero chemical potential. The first term, $\frac{8\pi h u^3}{c^3}$, represents the density of states for photons in a 3D cavity multiplied by the energy of a single photon $h u$. The second term, $\frac{1}{e^{$\frac{h u}{k_B T}$} - 1}$, is the Bose-Einstein distribution function, giving the average number of photons per mode at a given frequency and temperature.
plancks-law-for-spectral-energy-density-.symmetry_origin: The derivation relies on the statistical mechanics of a system of indistinguishable particles (photons) in thermal equilibrium. The black body itself is an idealized system that is isotropic and homogeneous in its emission/absorption properties. The concept of energy quantization $E=h u$ breaks classical continuous energy symmetry. The Bose-Einstein statistics arise from the indistinguishability of photons, a fundamental symmetry property of identical particles.
plancks-law-for-spectral-energy-density-.limits_and_boundary: When $h$ u \ll k_B T$ (low frequency / high temperature limit), Planck's law reduces to the Rayleigh-Jeans law: $u_ u($T$) \approx $\frac{8\pi u^2 k_B T}{c^3}$. This classical approximation accurately describes the spectrum at low frequencies but diverges at high frequencies, leading to the 'ultraviolet catastrophe.' When $h$ u \gg k_B T$(high frequency / low temperature limit), Planck's law reduces to Wien's approximation:$u_ u($T$) \approx $\frac{8\pi h u^3}{c^3}$ e^{-$\frac{h u}{k_B T}$}$. This approximation accurately describes the spectrum at high frequencies. Integrating $u_$ u($T$)$ over all frequencies yields the total energy density, which is proportional to $T^4$ (Stefan-Boltzmann Law). The frequency $u_{max}$ at which $u_$ u($T$)$ peaks is directly proportional to the absolute temperature $T$ (Wien's Displacement Law).

u_nu(T).name: Spectral Energy Density
u_nu(T).description: The energy per unit volume per unit frequency interval of electromagnetic radiation within a black-body cavity at temperature $T$.

h.name: Planck Constant
h.description: A fundamental physical constant representing the quantum of action, relating the energy of a photon to its frequency.

nu.name: Frequency
nu.description: The number of cycles per unit time of the electromagnetic wave.

c.name: Speed of Light in Vacuum
c.description: A universal physical constant representing the speed at which electromagnetic waves propagate in a vacuum.

k_B.name: Boltzmann Constant
k_B.description: A fundamental physical constant relating the average kinetic energy of particles in a gas with the thermodynamic temperature of the gas.

T.name: Absolute Temperature
T.description: The thermodynamic temperature of the black body in Kelvin.
